topics.title: Tricky rates problem
topics.text:
Inspired by Henry's IQ Question, I decided to pose a problem to AoPS's middle schoolers that actually tests IQ level.



ProblemTwo trains, Train A and Train B, are traveling toward each other on the same, straight track. (So their directions of travel are opposite each other) Train A is traveling at 35 miles per hour, while Train B is traveling at 25 miles per hour. Nothing special so far right? Well guess what. . . a hummingbird is sitting on the nose of Train A.



When the two trains are exactly 180 miles apart, the hummingbird takes off from Train A and flies directly toward Train B. As soon as it reaches Train B, it turns around and flies back to Train A. It continues this bizarre flight pattern until the two trains collide.

The hummingbird has a peculiar way of flying. It flies at exactly 40 miles per hour the entire time it is in the air.



So now, dear reader, how far did the hummingbird travel before the trains met their disastrous end? (and presumably the hummingbird too, sadly :( )




If you've seen this before try not to give it away right away. ;)

topics.title: A pretty quick way of computing sum of die
topics.text: I read about this strategy and I thought I would share it because some people don't know of it. You are given this question: How many ways can you roll a 7 using 3 die. Most people would do casework but here's an alternate way using sticks and stones. So you have 7 stones and 2 sticks, 9 slots in total. You have to subtract off 3 cases, where a stick is at the front back or adjacent to another.(loooooolo, oooolooool, olloooooo) because they give us 2 rolls not 3. This gives us 6 slots and 2 sticks so 6c2=15 sums. You can use this to find the probability of rolling a seven or just how many rolls in general. You can use this for bigger cases. 11 as sum 4 rolls. You must, however, be aware that some cases may give you a number that is bigger than 6 on a certain roll. Example; olooooooolo. The second roll is not possible since you cant roll 7 so watch out for that. I'll leave you with this for practice. The numbers 1-10 are in a bag and draw randomly with replacement. How many ways can you draw 4 numbers whose sum is 14?

The next step to actually takes self initiative. You need to go ahead of your class. You need to learn from outside resources. There are many on this website itself.

topics.title: Slip, slide and divide quadratic trick
topics.text:
In school today my teacher thought us some trick on how to factor quadratic so where the coefficient of $x^2$ is not 1. Quadratic formula still may be faster for some but it looks like an interesting alternate way. Hopefully this will help someone  :D

Steps1. Take the coefficient of the $x^2$ term and move it to the constant term(multiply it by the constant term)

2. Your quadratic  now looks like this $x^2+bx+ac$. Factor this like normal

3. Divide each root by the original coefficient of the $x^2$ term (so if it is factored as $(x-v_1)(x-v_2)$ then make it $\left(x-\frac{v_1}{a}\right)\left(x-\frac{v_2}{a}\right)$

4. Now put the coefficient  of $x^2$ outside of the factored quadratic. So $a\left(x-\frac{v_1}{a}\right)\left(x-\frac{v_2}{a}\right)$


Here is a walkthrough of me using it in a problem ProblemFactor $2x^2-5x+2$

First we move the coefficient of $x^2$ to get $x^2-5x+4$. This clearly factors as $(x-4)(x-1)$. Now divide the two roots by 2; $(x-2)\left(x-\frac{1}{2}\right)$. Now distribute the 2 in to make it $2(x-2)\left(x-\frac{1}{2}\right)$ and to get rid of the fraction, distribute the 2 into the second binomial to achieve $(x-2)(2x-1)$


And here is the proof for people who don't believe this ProofFirst let our quadratic be $ax^2+bx+c$. Now let the two roots of this be $v_1$ and $v_2$ so the quadratic can be factored as $a(x-v_1)(x-v_2)$. Also remember that $\frac{-b}{a}=v_1+v_2$ and $\frac{c}{a}=v_1v_2$. Easy manipulations make the two equations into $b=-a(v_1+v_2)$ and $c=v_1v_2a$.



The first step of slip, slide and divide is to make the quadratic $x^2+bx+ac$ plugging in our values for $b$ and $c$ we get; $x^2-ax(v_1+v_2)+v_1v_2a^2$. This can be factored as $(x-v_1a)(x-v_2a)$. The next step of slip, slide and divide is two divide the two roots by $a$. Doing so yields $\left(x-\frac{v_1a}{a}\right)\left(x-\frac{v_2a}{a}\right)=(x-v_1)(x-v_2)$. Now we stick $a$ on the outside to get $a(x-v_1)(x-v_2)$, completing our proof
